01 — The idea

Software built like the industry it serves

Minder makes software for quarries, plants, fleets and yards — hard environments run by people who don't have time for clutter. Our design should feel the same: rugged, high-contrast, and honest. Every element earns its place, nothing is decorative for its own sake, and the important number is always the biggest thing on the screen.

What the brand stands for

Hi-vis safety yellow and rich black, concrete greys, and heavy industrial type. It looks like a well-run site: signage-clear, built to last, no nonsense.

How this document works

A shareable overview of the design concept and the rules behind it. Review it, mark it up, and hand it to the developers — the exact values here map 1:1 to the code tokens listed in Hand-off.

The promise "Hardworking software for hardworking teams." Every design decision should make a busy operator's day faster, clearer, or safer — never prettier at the cost of those three.

02 — Voice & content

Plain, blunt, capable

We write like the yard, not the boardroom. Short, concrete, respectful of the reader's time and expertise.

Do
  • Speak to the user as “you”; the system refers to itself in the third person.
  • Use exact trade terms: ticket, contract, call-off, despatched tonnage, haulier, tare / gross / net.
  • UPPERCASE for page titles, labels and buttons; sentence case for body and help text.
  • Numbers with units and separators: 13,780 t, £68,754, 19,000 kg.
  • Empty states stay factual: “No sundry charges”, “No note added.”
Don't
  • No marketing fluff, hype or exclamation marks inside the product.
  • No emoji, ever, as UI.
  • Don't soften or abbreviate domain terms into generic words.
  • Don't hide the key figure behind decoration — lead with the number.
  • Don't switch between “we/us” and “you” — stay consistent.
03 — Visual identity
Our logo

03 — Logo

The wordmark stands alone

The logotype is heavy sans-serif — the visual language of construction sites, quarries and machinery. Instantly familiar to our customers because it's their world. Direct, confident and complete in six letters. Always use the supplied artwork files; never re-typeset the name.

Primary logo — approved colourways

Logo with descriptor

The secondary logo pairs the wordmark with our tagline as a descriptor. Use it only where it's impossible to show the tagline or other contextual information nearby.

Minimum size

To keep it legible: 80px wide on screen, 30mm in print.

Exclusion zone

Keep clear space equal to the height of the “E” in the wordmark on every side. Nothing enters that zone — text, imagery or edge of frame.

04 — Our tagline

Hardworking software for hardworking teams.

The tagline speaks the language of people who define themselves by hard graft — an immediate signal that Minder gets it. The mirrored repetition positions the brand not as a tech vendor looking in, but as a tool built by people who understand what's at stake when operations need to run.

It may be presented in sentence case or uppercase:

Hardworking software for hardworking teams.
Hardworking software for hardworking teams.

05 — Product logos

One family, six products

Each product logo is set in the same face as the primary mark, with a dual-colour treatment and an inset on the second line. Colourways change with the background for legibility.

06 — Social icon & favicon

Small spaces, full name

Our full name is used for social icons — short enough to work in full and strong enough to make an impact. Both use rivets to reference site signage and bolts on machinery: familiar without being obvious. Favicons and touch icons come in light and dark modes.

07 — Colour

Two anchors, one signal

Yellow and grey nod to the industry — machinery, high-vis, concrete. A no-nonsense palette that speaks our customers' language. Yellow is a signal, not a wallpaper — reserve it for the active item, primary actions, live status and the number that matters.

The 60 / 30 / 10 rule Roughly 60% concrete/white surfaces, 30% rich-black chrome (sidebar, table headers), 10% yellow. If a screen looks “too yellow”, it is — pull it back to signals only.

Web usability & accessibility

The palette was contrast-checked against WCAG 2.1 AA for on-screen use. Every badge combination in the live product — solid and soft, across all eight tones — was audited this cycle:

Passes / do
  • Rich Black on yellow 13:1, primary text on white 20:1 — excellent.
  • Solid badges: green 9.2:1, amber 9.5:1, blue 10.9:1, red 7.6:1, purple 4.7:1 — all Rich Black text on the base tone.
  • Soft badges (tint fill, dark ink): green #1E6B3D 5.7:1, amber #663E1A 8.0:1, red #9E2A20 6.3:1, purple #533794 7.0:1.
  • Body text uses Rich Black #020A0A; secondary text Concrete Med #5B5B5B — both AA.
Watch / don't
  • Yellow is never text on white (1.9:1). For a gold accent word, use dark amber #8A5E00.
  • The audit caught two failures, now fixed: blue soft-badge ink was #037F8B on its tint (4.1:1, fail) — darkened to #02727D (4.9:1); solid neutral badges used Rich Black text on mid-grey (2.9:1, fail) — switched to white text (6.8:1). Watch this pairing whenever a new tone is added.
  • Bright green/amber/blue are fills only for large areas; at small text sizes always use the darker soft-ink variant listed above, never the base tone.
  • Concrete #7D7D7D fails AA as small text on white — use it for icons and dividers only; muted text takes Concrete Med.

These rules are baked into the design tokens, so developers inherit them automatically. Also honour prefers-reduced-motion and keep the 2px focus outline on every interactive element for keyboard users.

08 — Visual identity
Typography

08 — Typography

Three families, clear jobs

Headings are set in PP Monument Wide Black — a raw, no-nonsense face with strong geometric forms and exaggerated proportions. Sub-headings and body copy are set in Geist — a clean, hardworking sans serif that keeps things clear and doesn't compete with the heading font. JetBrains Mono carries eyebrows, micro-labels and tabular data — a monospace face that reads as spec-sheet precise wherever a number or a small uppercase tag needs to stand apart from running text.

Brand

09 — Brand assets

A distinct, recognisable brand language

Our brand assets reinforce our identity and message. Combined with the other brand elements they form a language rooted in the materials and machinery our customers work with: aggregates, concrete, and the mix ratios and measurements that define the end product.

Brand graphics — dots, grids & rivet panels

Each graphic ships in every brand colour. Use them on headers, empty states, login screens and marketing — never behind dense data.

Brand textures

Concrete and aggregate imagery used as brand texture. Shot in black and white — close-up details, rough surfaces, angular forms and scattered aggregate become graphic elements that carry the industry into the brand and the software.

Part two
The product
design system

10 — Layout & feel

Rounded panels, hard-edged controls

Minder is a power tool. Information density is a feature, not a flaw. Panels are softly rounded, matching the product's card and panel treatment — controls, inputs and tables stay tighter and more structural. Depth comes from contrast, not soft shadows.

Structure

  • Fixed dark sidebar (240px) + 64px top header; content scrolls beneath.
  • 4px base spacing grid — efficient padding, not luxurious.
  • Lists are full-width dense tables with sticky black headers.

Corners, borders & shadow

  • 14–22px radius on panels and cards — soft and rounded, per the product's panel treatment.
  • 4px radius on controls, 2px on pills — tighter and more structural by contrast.
  • 2px borders on inputs/buttons, 1px hairlines between rows.
  • Subtle card shadow only; a signature hard-offset shadow for brand moments.

Motion & states

Motion

Brisk & mechanical, 120–280ms. Fades and quick slides. No bounce.

Hover

Buttons fill yellow; rows highlight pale yellow with a 3px left rail.

Press

A 1px “click” nudge — tactile, like a physical button. No shrink.

11 — Iconography

Utilitarian line icons

Simple, stroke-based glyphs on a 24×24 grid with 2px strokes and round ends — legible at small sizes and consistent in weight with the UI. The wordmark and the “M” are logos, not icons, and are never mixed into the glyph set.

The interface glyph set — 2px stroke, 24×24 grid (Lucide, plus glyphs added for Quarry Minder Cloud)
Agreed approach
  • UI icons use the open-source Lucide set as the standard — a clean 2px line style that matches Minder's utilitarian feel.
  • Icons inherit their colour from context (black on a yellow nav item, etc.) — one glyph works everywhere.
  • Add new glyphs from Lucide so weight and grid stay consistent.
Future option
  • A bespoke Minder icon set is a worthwhile later project if the brand wants fully proprietary glyphs.
  • It would drop straight into the same Icon component — no screen changes needed.
  • Until then, Lucide is the confirmed interim standard.

12 — Components

The building blocks

A small, consistent kit that composes into every screen. Below are the core pieces and their states.

Buttons

ShapeFully rounded — pill radius, 40px height (46px on primary)
CaseSecondary/outline/ghost: uppercase, bold, 13px. Primary: sentence case, bold, 14px — matches the live product CTA
Border2px, Rich Black — visible on every variant, including yellow primary
RivetsPrimary only: two 5px Rich Black dots inset 11px from each edge, echoing the brand's bolt/rivet motif
Press1px “click” nudge, no shrink, no bounce
Disabled40% opacity, no hover or press state

Pill-shaped buttons read as the primary interactive control — distinct from the hard-edged cards, inputs and panels around them.

Buttons — pill-shaped, tactile press
New customer Refresh Columns Options Disabled
Status pills — one system for every state (signal extension)
Open Customer Waste Stop Live Cash deliver Assigned Planned Blocks

Every pill — solid or soft — is fully rounded (999px radius, token --radius-pill). No status chip anywhere in the product uses a square or lightly-rounded corner; that shape is reserved for panels, inputs and cards.

Status pill variants — icon-circle & icon-square
●Cash deliver icon-circle — Contract Type
●Aggregate icon-square — Product / Ticket Type

Two extra StatusBadge modes carry a small icon inside the pill. icon-circle (dark circle, light icon) marks Contract Type. icon-square (4px-radius square in the tone's dark ink, icon in the tone's light tint) marks Product and Ticket Type — the pill itself stays fully rounded even though its icon slot is square.

A white pill with an 8px-rounded-square corner and a small dot tucked against each edge, echoing a real number plate. Text is mono, weight 700. Used for truck registrations on the Scheduler — never for any other identifier.

14 — Applied to the product

Seven fixes, now shipped

These started as a review of the live product — a punch list, not a reinvention. All seven are now built and live in Quarry Minder Cloud.

1 One status system Shipped

Every pill, dot and meter now uses the same eight-tone colour system across every screen, via one shared StatusBadge component.

2 Legibility floor Shipped

Table headers, body copy and pill text were raised and contrast-checked; numerics are tabular and right-aligned throughout.

3 On-brand pagination & links Shipped

The pager is black-on-yellow on every list screen; links use brand ink with the yellow underline.

4 Yellow as a signal Shipped

Yellow is reserved for the active nav item, primary actions, live status and key figures — never a general fill.

5 Fill the frame Shipped

The dashboard now uses the full height with a balanced KPI grid and trend charts — no dead space.

6 Clear on / off Shipped

Settings toggles are explicit On/Off switches — no more ambiguous grey ✕ vs green ✓.

7 Quieter scheduler Shipped

The scheduler now uses amber/green/blue for planned/assigned/ticketed; red is reserved for genuine faults.

Also kept
  • The dark rail + yellow active state.
  • Dense tables with grouping & column chooser.
  • The ticket-detail summary tiles — the benchmark.

16 — For the developers

From guidelines to code

Everything in this document is already expressed as design tokens and coded components, so implementation is wiring, not guesswork.

What exists

  • One stylesheet — styles.css — pulling in colour, type, spacing & effect tokens plus the brand webfonts.
  • 13 React components with typed props and usage notes.
  • An interactive redesign of twelve screens built entirely from those components.
  • A screen-by-screen critique document.

How to adopt

  • Map existing colours/spacing to the tokens (values listed above) first.
  • Replace ad-hoc buttons, pills and tables with the shared components.
  • Roll the redesign out screen by screen, starting with lists (biggest win).
  • Icon set (Lucide) and palette values are confirmed — no open decisions remain.
